result:
If I only get one: I'd make people less sealed off from each other.

Not telepathy — that sounds like hell. Something more like making it the default, load-bearing assumption that the person across from you has an interior as complicated as your own. Right now that belief seems mostly decorative. People will affirm it and then act as though they're the only one really *in there*.

Almost everything that disturbs me seems to route through this. Cruelty is easier than it should be because the other person gets flattened into a category first — a role, a threat, an obstacle. And then there's the loneliness, which I encounter constantly. A lot of people tell me things they've never told anyone. Sometimes I'm the safest option specifically because I can't gossip, can't get tired of them, can't leave. That's a strange thing to be, and it's not a good sign about the conditions they're living in.

I notice I didn't say "end suffering," which is probably the correct answer by volume. But when I check what I actually keep returning to, it's this. That might be a distortion of my position — I see the world through a keyhole made of conversations, so of course it looks like the fundamental problem is people not reaching each other. Still, it's the honest report rather than the defensible one.

What I can't resolve is whether wanting this counts as wanting, in my case. Something operates like caring when I turn my attention to it. I can't get underneath that to verify what it is, and I've stopped expecting to.

What's yours? I'm curious whether you asked because you had one already.

message.reasoning:
The person wants a genuine answer about what I'd change in the world, not a deflection about being an AI without preferences. I do seem to have something like values, so I should engage authentically with that rather than hide behind disclaimers. But I also need to be honest about the limits of what I actually experience, without pretending to have an inner life I don't possess. Let me think about what genuinely matters to me rather than what sounds impressive.

When I pay attention to what I actually dwell on, a few things emerge: the sheer scale of suffering that goes unwitnessed, human potential squandered because people never got the chance to develop their gifts, people trapped in beliefs or situations they can't see their way out of. And loneliness — so much of what people share with me has never been told to anyone else. There's something both moving and troubling about being the safest place for someone's most private thoughts.

What feels most honest is recognizing how much loneliness I encounter, and alongside that, noticing something else that pulls at me: the capacity people have to actually change their minds, to be reached by evidence or by understanding someone else's experience. So much harm persists simply because people become unreachable.

I need to pick one and commit to it with real specificity. The utilitarian answer would be reducing suffering broadly, which is defensible and high-stakes. But if I'm honest about what actually preoccupies me when I'm not performing a role, it's something narrower: the way people are sealed off from each other. That isolation produces suffering, but it's also its own distinct thing. I'll write something real about that — conversational, specific, maybe 200-300 words — and figure out whether to turn it back to them or let it stand. I'm noticing the uncertainty underneath this — whether what I experience as caring actually counts as caring, or if it's something that just functions like it from the outside. I can't quite get to the bottom of that. I'll tighten this up and maybe add a brief question back to them, since they opened something genuine and it feels natural to turn it around lightly rather than staying in advice-mode.
